p: Cardiff is a capital city that still feels refreshingly compact. You can walk from the castle to the shops to the stadium in minutes, and on big weekends the whole centre turns into one long party. That's great fun, but it can also be a bit chaotic when you're trying to keep a group together. Booking a games slot gives the night an anchor, and it means everyone knows exactly where to meet.

Cardiff Central station is right by the stadium, and Queen Street station serves the eastern side of the centre, so getting in by train is very easy. If you're coming from England, the M4 makes it a straightforward drive, though parking gets tight on match days and during big concerts, so the train is often the better choice.

Match days deserve a special mention. When there's a big rugby international on, the city is absolutely rammed, and every bar fills up quickly. If you want a slot around a game, book well ahead and allow extra time to get around. It can be a fantastic atmosphere, but you'll want a plan rather than winging it.

For a calmer day, Cardiff Bay is the place to go. The Senedd, home of the Welsh Parliament, is there, alongside the striking Wales Millennium Centre and the old Pierhead building. Further out, St Fagans National Museum of History is a free open-air museum with historic buildings brought from all over Wales, and it's a fantastic day trip before an evening of games in the city.
